source.citation: Wang W., Du Z., Deng S., et al. Regeneration of PFOS loaded activated carbon by hot water and subsequent aeration enrichment of PFOS from eluent. Carbon. 2018;134:199–206. (EPA HERO summary).

evidence_passages.passage: Regeneration and reuse of spent activated carbon (AC) as well as recovery of the desorbed pollutants are challenging in the application of adsorption technology. In this study, the regeneration of perfluorooctanesulfonate (PFOS)-saturated coal-based granular AC by hot water and subsequent aeration method to enrich PFOS from eluent were investigated.

source_limitations: The HERO entry largely mirrors the journal abstract and does not add quantitative performance or detailed operating conditions beyond what is captured in WEB70; it is retained here as an independent regulatory summary but is redundant for many technical parameters.

sources.citation: Liu B., Chen J., You Y., Sun M. Cyclic removal and destruction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances from water using ion exchange, resin regeneration, and UV/sulfite reduction. Water Research. 2025;272:122915.

evidence_chunks.text: Using the proposed treatment train (IX → resin regeneration → distillation of waste regenerant → UV/sulfite treatment of still bottoms), PFAS at environmentally relevant levels (1000 ng/L) with different chain lengths and functional groups can be effectively removed to near 100 %, using either PFAS-specific or generic resins, and eventually defluorinated in UPW, SW, and GW.

The optimized treatment train includes IX, resin regeneration with 5 wt % NaCl and 60 % v/v methanol, distillation of waste regenerant, and advanced reduction by hydrated electrons (eaq−) generated during the ultraviolet/sulfite (UV/sulfite) treatment of still bottoms.
Regenerated resins had comparable PFAS removal to pristine resins over three cycles.

evidence_chunks.text: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are being detected frequently in water, raising health concerns. While anion exchange resins (IERs) are effective in removing PFAS contamination in water to below regulatory limits (often in the ng/L range), their regeneration efficiency is typically low, requiring high-salinity brines that generate substantial secondary waste and limit reuse over multiple cycles.

The study title and repository record indicate a treatment train that couples cyclic sorption and regeneration of ion exchange resins with UV/sulfite treatment to achieve complete PFOS removal, implying evaluation of repeated adsorption–regeneration cycles and destructive treatment of regenerant streams.

evidence_chunks.text: Three resins – A592E and USA291597EPF (strong base resins) and USA21107 (weak base resin) – were evaluated using aqueous and organic solvent regenerants across multiple cycles. Batch regeneration experiments demonstrated that regeneration effectiveness was higher for short chain perfluoroalkyl carboxylates (PFCA) compared to long chain PFCA, followed by n:2 fluorotelomer sulfonates (FtS) and perfluoroalkane sulfonates (PFSA).

Organic solvent regenerants outperformed aqueous solutions, with effectiveness increasing at higher percentages. For low organic solvent percentages, acetone demonstrated higher effectiveness compared to ethanol and methanol.
The findings highlight the crucial role of regenerant composition in optimizing resin regeneration, offering valuable insights for developing more effective PFAS remediation strategies.

evidence_chunks.text: The scCO2-amended with ethanol and HCl achieves rapid and near-complete regeneration of PFOA-loaded resins, RE% = 99.7 ± 0.1% at T = 75 °C and a 60 min contact time, without compromising their structure or surface functional groups, thus enabling repeated adsorption-regeneration cycles.

The PFAS-rich regenerant is then fully mineralized in a continuous-flow supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) system, where the regenerant's chemical energy enables the reactor's autogenic operation, eliminating secondary waste streams.

Integrating rapid PFAS extraction and downstream PFAS destruction enables the reuse of IXR sorbents and reduces treatment costs, material consumption, and long-term environmental liability in PFAS remediation.

sources.citation: Gagliano E., Falciglia P.P., Zaker Y., Karanfil T., Roccaro P. Microwave regeneration of granular activated carbon saturated with PFAS. Water Research. 2021;198:117121.

evidence_chunks.text: This study investigated the regeneration of PFAS-saturated granular activated carbons (GACs) by microwave (MW) irradiation. Two commercially available GACs (bituminous coal based GAC [BCGAC] and lignite coal based GAC [LCGAC]) were saturated with perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) and then irradiated at different MW conditions (applied power = 125–500 W, irradiation time = 3–12 min).

The performance of MW regeneration for PFOS- or PFOA-saturated GACs was assessed by evaluating the variation of GAC adsorption capacity (regeneration efficiency, RE) and weight loss percentage (WL). Moreover, the effect of MW irradiation on GAC textural properties (e.g., surface area and pore volume) was examined through N2 adsorption isotherms.

sources.citation: Ranjbar E., Ahmadi F., Baghdadi M. Regeneration of perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) loaded granular activated carbon using organic/inorganic mixed solutions. Chemical Engineering Science. 2024;300:120623.

evidence_chunks.text: Herein, regeneration of PFAS-saturated GAC was studied and organic/inorganic mixed solutions were used to regenerate exhausted GAC. Optimization experiments revealed that a regenerant solution consisting of 0.1 mol/L HCl in ethanol with a 30-min residence time effectively regenerated PFAS-saturated GAC.

The results showed that even after the fifth usage cycle, the proposed regeneration method can efficiently regenerate the PFAS-saturated GAC. Identification of the regeneration mechanism indicated that the regeneration process can be attributed to physical displacement and solubilization of PFAS from exhausted GAC.

Additionally, BET analysis of PFAS-saturated and regenerated GACs revealed an increase in total pore volume and BET surface area in regenerated GACs, demonstrating the suggested method’s regeneration capabilities.

sources.citation: Wang W., Du Z., Deng S., Vakili M., Ren L., Meng P., et al. Regeneration of PFOS loaded activated carbon by hot water and subsequent aeration enrichment of PFOS from eluent. Carbon. 2018;134:199–206.

evidence_chunks.text: In this study, the regeneration of perfluorooctanesulfonate (PFOS)-saturated coal-based granular AC by hot water and subsequent aeration method to enrich PFOS from eluent were investigated. The regeneration time, water temperature and solid-liquid ratio affected the regeneration efficiency of PFOS treated AC.

PFOS was desorbed quickly from the AC within 30 min by hot water. High water temperature (92 °C) and low solid-liquid ratio (0.5) led to the highest desorption of 36.7% in one cycle (6 h). Over 90% PFOS on the spent AC was desorbed by 92 °C hot water with the solid-liquid ratio of 0.5 after six cycles.

Aeration of the regeneration eluent achieved enrichment factors of 50.6–62.0 for PFOS at initial PFOS concentrations of 10–100 μg/L. The concentration of PFOS in the concentrated solution was 2.2 g/L following sequential sorption, regeneration and aeration treatments when the influent PFOS concentration was 2.7 μg/L.

source_limitations: Only abstract text was accessed; detailed adsorption capacities before and after regeneration, GAC structural characterization, and any decline in capacity across cycles are not visible.
The study recovers PFOS into a concentrated liquid; no destructive treatment or lifecycle analysis of this concentrate is provided on the inspected page.

evidence_chunks.text: The pilot test compared ion exchange resin to granular activated carbon (GAC) and evaluated in-place regeneration of the resin to restore PFAS removal capacity.

Compared at a common empty bed contact time (EBCT) of five minutes, the resin treated over eight times as many bed volumes (BVs) of groundwater as GAC before PFOS exceeded the USEPA health advisory and six times as many BVs for PFOA.

A solution of organic solvent and brine was used to regenerate the resin in the lead vessel, which had treated water up to the point of PFOS and PFOA breakthrough exceeding the USEPA HAs. The pilot test demonstrated successful in-place regeneration of the resin to near-virgin conditions. The regenerated resin was then used to treat the contaminated groundwater up to the same breakthrough point.

evidence_chunks.text: After the GAC has reached the end of its useful service life and become “spent carbon,” it is common practice in industry to thermally treat it in a process known as reactivation. The reactivation process volatilizes and destroys adsorbed contaminants at high temperatures and restores the GAC to a near-virgin state so that it can be reused.
These data demonstrate that reactivation of PFAS-laden GAC in a facility operating a multihearth furnace with appropriate abatement results in high levels of destruction of PFAS compounds.
Targeted PFAS analysis is reported in ng/g (ppb) scale while fluoride measurements are at µg/g (ppm) or ppm by volume scale for carbon and gas-phase fluoride testing, respectively.

sources.citation: Lin Z., Doudrick K., Herckes P., Chester M., Westerhoff P., Boyer T.H. Life cycle assessment of the thermal oxidation and pyrolysis of granular activated carbon loaded with perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS). Journal of Cleaner Production. 2025;501:145325.

evidence_chunks.text: The spent GAC can be thermally destroyed or regenerated for reuse. To understand how innovations in thermal treatment can reduce environmental impact of PFAS-laden GAC, we performed a life cycle assessment (LCA) of the thermal oxidation and pyrolysis of perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) loaded onto GAC with and without the use of calcium additives.

Without an additive, the LCA indicated that regeneration and reuse have an overall lower environmental impact than thermal oxidation. The highest impact comes from the need for an afterburner to treat the volatile organic fluorine (VOF).

Using hydrated lime as an additive decreases the temperature and time required for mineralization of PFAS, reducing the environmental impact in all categories. This is attributed to not needing post-processes to handle VOF and HF.

source_limitations: Only the abstract and highlights were available; detailed inventory data (energy, reagents, emissions) and assumptions about regeneration performance and PFOS mineralization are not visible.

sources.citation: Soker O., Tajdini B., Abarca-Perez A., Strathmann T.J., et al. Reuse of spent granular activated carbon for PFAS removal following hydrothermal alkaline treatment. Water Research. 2025;283:123794.

evidence_chunks.text: This study investigates spent GAC regeneration by hydrothermal alkaline treatment (HALT), which applies subcritical water (e.g., 350 °C, 16.5 MPa) amended with strong base (e.g., NaOH) to destroy PFAS.

This study presents data from rapid small-scale column tests (RSSCTs) demonstrating effective removal of long-chain PFAS by a HALT-treated spent GAC sample collected from a long-term PFAS treatment field pilot study (BV50 > 50,000 for PFOS, PFHxS, and PFNA).

Analyses of reactor liquid products, media mass loss, and NaOH neutralization by GAC also provided evidence for removal of adsorbed non-target organic matter and possible GAC surface renewal by carbon gasification reactions occurring in parallel with PFAS destruction, analogous to surface carbon burn-off that occurs during high-temperature thermal reactivation.
